# effect-spacetimedb 0.8.0

A breaking release. The required `effect` peer moves to the stable `^4.1.1`
line and the required `spacetimedb` peer to `~2.14.0`, which also makes a
reducer's `senderAuth` a union of three states and needs one more host import
kept external. Every `Stdb.array` states how many elements it may carry, every
client connection states how long it may wait, the call-failure unions gain
two errors, and the dev server publishes with an environment it builds itself
instead of the one it runs in. It adds database environments, SDK automatic
reconnect, views that take arguments and inter-database calls. Nothing on the
wire moved for the views you already have, so a 0.8.0 client and a 0.7.0
module still speak the same protocol.

## Breaking changes

### Migrating from 0.7

#### Move `effect` to the stable `4.1.1` line

0.8.0 requires `effect@^4.1.1` (and `@effect/atom-react@^4.1.1` for the React
entry point). 0.7.0 imports `effect/unstable/*`, which the stable line removed,
so 0.7.0 does not load on `effect@latest`; 0.8.0 is the first release that
does, and it no longer loads on the 4.0 release candidates.

```sh
npm install effect-spacetimedb@0.8.0 effect@4.1.1 spacetimedb@2.14.0
```

Code you write against this package moves with it. The Effect modules its
types expose and its examples import left `effect/unstable`:

| With 0.7 (`effect@4.0.0-rc.117`)         | With 0.8 (`effect@4.1.1`)        |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `effect/unstable/http/HttpClient`        | `effect/http/HttpClient`         |
| `effect/unstable/httpapi/HttpApiClient`  | `effect/http-api/HttpApiClient`  |
| `effect/unstable/reactivity/AsyncResult` | `effect/reactivity/AsyncResult`  |
| `effect/unstable/<area>/<Module>`        | `effect/<area>/<Module>`         |

Other stable-line renames that reach code built on this package:
`Schema.isLengthBetween` is `Schema.isBetweenLength` (the size, property and
string checks follow the same subject-last or grammatical spelling),
`effect/Encoding` splits into `effect/encoding/Base64`, `Base64Url` and `Hex`,
`effect/Crypto` becomes `effect/crypto/SecureRandom` and `Digest`, and HTTP
request methods are typed as `string`. The lower bound is 4.1.1 rather than
4.1.0 because 4.1.0's crypto declarations fail to typecheck under
`@types/node` 22 or 24 without the DOM library.

Effect 4.1 builds a `TextDecoder` with the `ignoreBOM` option while its HTTP
and encoding modules load, and the SpaceTimeDB module host's decoder rejects
that option, so a module failed to load once its import graph reached those
modules. `effect-spacetimedb/server-polyfills` now supplies the option on such
a host. `server-compiler` still installs the polyfills, but a module entry that
reaches Effect's HTTP modules before it, for example through a shared contract
declaring `HttpApi` routes, must import `effect-spacetimedb/server-polyfills`
as its first import.

#### Move the `spacetimedb` peer to `~2.14.0`, and match your CLI to it

```sh
npm install effect-spacetimedb@0.8.0 spacetimedb@2.14.0 effect@4.1.1
```

Generate bindings with a `spacetime` CLI of the same version: the module-def
format is patch-version coupled, and `effect-spacetimedb/codegen` refuses any
other CLI with `CodegenCliVersionError`. Publish to a 2.14 host as well: a
module built against the 2.14 SDK reads the sender a 2.14 host passes to every
HTTP handler, so on an older host each of its HTTP routes fails when called,
while its reducers keep working and its publish succeeds.

From SpacetimeDB 2.13.0 an HTTP reducer call with confirmed reads (the
server's default) is answered only once its transaction is durable, and one
whose durability is not confirmed within five seconds is answered `504`,
which the HTTP client surfaces as a
`RemoteRejectedError` with `status: 504`. Treat that as "outcome unknown",
like a `TransportError`: the transaction may have committed. A procedure's
`withTx` now waits for durability the same way (always, for scheduled
procedures and HTTP handlers); when that wait times out the host stops the
procedure right after the commit, discards the instance, and an HTTP caller
gets `500`. The commit stands, and the rest of the procedure did not run.

Since 2.12 the SDK's `spacetimedb/server` imports a third host module,
`spacetime:sys@2.2` (behind database environments), beside `spacetime:sys@2.0`
and `@2.1`. Native `spacetime build` handles it. A bundler you run yourself
over a module entry must keep it external along with the other two, and
off-host tests that import `spacetimedb/server` must alias it to the stub:
`spacetimeSysAlias` from `effect-spacetimedb/testing` now maps all three to
`effect-spacetimedb/testing/spacetime-sys`, so only a hand-written alias list
needs the new entry.

Three defects remain in the published `spacetimedb` 2.14.0 package, and an npm
install does not fix them for you. This repository ships the fix as
[`patches/spacetimedb@2.14.0.patch`](https://github.com/miragegame/effect-spacetimedb/blob/main/patches/spacetimedb@2.14.0.patch).
Its paths are relative to the `spacetimedb` package root, so Bun applies it as
a `patchedDependencies` entry in your root `package.json`:

```json
{
  "patchedDependencies": {
    "spacetimedb@2.14.0": "patches/spacetimedb@2.14.0.patch"
  }
}
```

pnpm takes the same entry under `pnpm.patchedDependencies` in `package.json`
or `patchedDependencies` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`; other package managers need
their own patch mechanism. The entry matches only `spacetimedb` 2.14.0, so pin
that version, and apply it wherever the SDK is installed: module and client
packages alike. What it fixes:

- The SDK's `Prettify` rewrites a branded primitive into a mapped object type.
  Upstream: https://github.com/clockworklabs/SpacetimeDB/pull/5971 (merged,
  not yet in a release).
- A client `TableCache` range over an `Identity`, `Timestamp` or other
  object-backed key compares the wrapper objects rather than their values.
  Upstream: https://github.com/clockworklabs/SpacetimeDB/pull/5970 (open).
- A non-unique index whose columns are a strict subset of a unique constraint
  is classified as unique, so it is built without its range methods.
  Upstream: https://github.com/clockworklabs/SpacetimeDB/pull/5969 (open).

#### A reducer's `senderAuth` is a union of three states

SpacetimeDB 2.14 makes a sender internal exactly when it is the database itself
(a scheduled reducer, or a scheduled procedure's transaction) and gives an
internal sender no JWT, so a reducer's `senderAuth` is now a union of the three
states that leaves: internal with no JWT, external with a JWT, and external
without one. The union is `ServerSenderAuth`, now exported as a type from
`effect-spacetimedb/server`. Checking `hasJWT` narrows
`jwt` to the claims, and a hand-built `senderAuth` must be one of the three:
`isInternal: true` beside a JWT, or a `hasJWT` that disagrees with `jwt`, no
longer compiles. The test harness's default `senderAuth` follows the same
rule, so a context whose `sender` is its `databaseIdentity` is internal unless
the test passes its own `senderAuth`.

#### `Stdb.array` requires length bounds

`Stdb.array(item)` no longer compiles. Pass inclusive bounds:

```ts
// 0.7
Stdb.array(Stdb.string())

// 0.8
Stdb.array(Stdb.string(), { minimum: 0, maximum: 64 })
```

Write `minimum: 0` when an empty array is normal and `1` when it is a bug, and
choose a `maximum` that is a real limit for your data rather than
`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Both bounds must be non-negative safe integers with
`minimum <= maximum`; anything else throws a `TypeError` when the type is
constructed.

The bounds are enforced when decoding and when encoding, on every transport:
reducer and procedure arguments, returns, table rows and view results. An
oversized value fails with `StdbHostEncodeError` (reason
`"ArrayLengthOutOfBounds"`, carrying `length` and `bounds`) before any element
is encoded, or with the schema decode error on the way in.
`Stdb.describe(type).length` exposes them.

Bounds never reach the wire. SATS `array<T>` has no length, so arrays that
differ only in their bounds lower to the same SATS type, fingerprint and
generated client type, and changing a bound is not a schema migration. That
cuts both ways for stored data: rows are decoded with the bounds of the module
that reads them, so tightening a bound on a table column (or on anything a row
nests) makes existing rows that exceed it fail to decode. Widen freely; tighten
only after checking or rewriting the stored rows.

Two type-level consequences for code that inspects the library's own types:
`StdbArrayDescriptor` (from `Stdb.describe`) now always carries `length`, and
`StdbHostEncodeError["reason"]` gains the `"ArrayLengthOutOfBounds"` member,
so an exhaustive match over encode-error reasons needs one more case.

`Stdb.bytes()` is unchanged; bound it through its schema
(`Schema.Uint8Array.check(Schema.isMaxLength(n))`).

#### Client connections require a time bound

HTTP clients take a new required `callDurationMax` (any `Duration.Input`), and
WebSocket connections now require `connectTimeoutMillis`, which 0.7 accepted
but let you omit:

```ts
// 0.7
Example.client.http.layer({ uri, databaseName, token })
Example.client.ws.layerGenerated({ DbConnection, uri, databaseName, token })

// 0.8
Example.client.http.layer({
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  callDurationMax: "10 seconds",
})
Example.client.ws.layerGenerated({
  DbConnection,
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
  connectTimeoutMillis: 10_000,
})
```

This applies to every HTTP constructor (`client.http.make`, `.layer` and
`.group`) and every WebSocket one (`client.ws.scoped`, `.scopedGenerated`,
`.layer`, `.layerGenerated`, and the session supervisors, which already
required the timeout). In 0.7 an HTTP call waited as long as the provided
`HttpClient` did, and a WebSocket acquisition without a timeout waited forever
if the native builder never invoked a connect callback; with no bound, a
partitioned or paused database held every caller indefinitely. There is no
library default, because the right bound is the caller's budget: a request
deadline, a lease, a heartbeat window.

- An HTTP call still unanswered at `callDurationMax`, response body included,
  fails with `TransportError` whose `cause` is `HttpCallDurationExceeded`
  (carrying `callName` and the bound). The bound stops the caller waiting, not
  the database: a request that already arrived may still commit, so treat a
  `TransportError` as "outcome unknown", never as "did not happen".
- A WebSocket acquisition still unfinished at `connectTimeoutMillis` fails with
  `WsConnectError` whose `cause` is `WsConnectTimeoutError`, and the half-built
  connection is disconnected.
- Both bounds must be positive and finite: constructing a client with an
  infinite, zero, negative or `NaN` bound throws a `TypeError`.

Per-call deadlines for WebSocket reducer and procedure calls are not part of
this release.

#### Call failures and supervisor phases gain cases

`CallFailure<E>` and `RawCallFailure<E>`, the error unions of every typed and
`.raw` reducer, procedure and HTTP-handler call, gain exactly two members, both
exported from the root and `effect-spacetimedb/client`:

- `CallNotSentError`: the call never left the client, because its session was
  reconnecting. Retrying once the session is live again is safe.
- `ConnectionIdentityChangedError`: an automatic reconnect came back under a
  different identity, so the session ended. No retry on that session can
  succeed; a new one needs credentials for the intended identity.

Only a WebSocket session with automatic reconnect (below) produces them, so a
client that does not opt in never sees them at runtime. Code that handles every
member still needs the two new cases to compile, for example a `catchTags`
whose result must fail with `never`, or a `Match.tagsExhaustive`. For the same
reason `WsSessionSupervisorPhase` gains a `recovering` status, which an
exhaustive `switch` over `phase.status` must handle.

#### The dev server builds the publishing CLI's environment

The `spacetime` CLI publishes any process variable named like a key the module
declares (see database environments, below), so the dev server no longer lets
it inherit yours. Every publish it runs (the first publish, `republish`,
`reset`, and the new `publishDatabase` and `updateEnvironment`) starts the CLI
with only the reserved base variables in `environmentKeysReserved` (`PATH`,
`HOME`, the temp and Windows profile directories, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` and
`SPACETIMEDB_SCHEMA_EXTRACTOR`), read from `processEnvironment` (default:
`process.env`), plus the database environment values you pass. Anything else a
publish relied on inheriting from your shell no longer reaches it.

- Publish, environment updates and delete run with `--no-config`, so a
  `spacetime.json` above the working directory no longer contributes values or
  targets.
- A supplied value or a module declaration whose key is one of the reserved
  names (compared case-insensitively) is refused before anything is published,
  with `DevServerReservedEnvironmentKeyError`.
- `reset` with a bundle is now one clearing publish (`--delete-data=always`),
  the host's own reset: it builds the bundle and runs `init` with the
  replacement values before it deletes anything, keeps the database's identity,
  and on any refusal leaves the database and its stored values as they were.
  0.7 deleted the database and then published, so a failing `init` left you
  with none. `DevServerResetVerificationError`, which reported a database still
  present after that delete, is gone: drop it from imports and matches.
- `DevServerError` gains `DevServerEnvironmentKeyError`,
  `DevServerReservedEnvironmentKeyError`, `DevServerEnvironmentValueError` and
  `DevServerDatabaseNameInUseError`, and `PublishedModuleRuntime` gains
  `databaseIdentity`, `updateEnvironment`, `remove` and `publishDatabase`; an
  exhaustive match over dev-server errors or a hand-written fake runtime needs
  the new members.

## New: database environments

SpacetimeDB 2.12 added per-database environment values that a publisher
supplies and the host validates before `init` or a migration runs. A module
now declares the keys it reads in its contract, and handlers read them through
the module's `Env` accessor. See
[Environment Variables](https://effect-stdb.dev/core-concepts/databases/environment-variables).

```ts
const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app", {
  environment: {
    API_KEY: Stdb.Environment.secret(),
    MODE: Stdb.Environment.literal("development", "production"),
    LOG_LEVEL: Stdb.Environment.optional(Stdb.Environment.literal("info", "debug")),
  },
}).add(Settings)
const { Env } = Module

describeSettings: Effect.fn(function* () {
  const env = yield* Env
  const mode = yield* env.MODE // "development" | "production"
  const apiKey = yield* env.API_KEY // Redacted<string>
  // ...
})
```

- `Stdb.Environment.string()`, `.secret()`, `.literal(...)` and
  `.optional(...)` declare keys. Declarations are checked against the host's
  limits when the contract is built (`StdbValidationError`), and only the
  declarations, never a value, reach the bundle.
- `Env` is available to every handler of a module that declares at least one
  key; a module that declares none keeps the handler types it had. Each key is
  an Effect that reads the host when it runs, uncached, so a read inside a
  transaction sees its snapshot. A secret reads back as `Redacted<string>`. A
  failed host read, or a value that contradicts its declaration, is a defect
  (`StdbEnvironmentHostReadDefect`, `StdbEnvironmentValueDefect`).
  `effect-spacetimedb/server` exports `Env` and `EnvService`.
- The module test harness takes `environment` values, refuses ones the host
  would refuse with `TestModuleEnvironmentError`, and changes them with
  `harness.updateEnvironment(...)`. Off-host code that calls the SDK's own
  `env_get` can be backed by the same values with `withEnvironment` or
  `withEnvironmentAsync` from `effect-spacetimedb/testing/spacetime-sys`.
- The dev server publishes `environment` values (pass secrets as `Redacted` so
  command diagnostics print `<redacted>`), checks them against the bundle's
  declarations first (`DevServerEnvironmentValueError`), and changes them
  without a module upload through
  `runtime.updateEnvironment(values, { unset })`.
  `republish(bundle, { environment })` and `reset({ environment })` take values
  too.

## New: automatic reconnect

SpacetimeDB 2.12's SDK can reconnect an established WebSocket connection by
itself, keeping one connection object, client cache, subscription handles and
callbacks across a dropped socket and replaying the subscriptions. Opt in with
`automaticReconnect` on any WebSocket config. Without it a dropped socket still
ends the session, as in 0.7. See
[Connection](https://effect-stdb.dev/core-concepts/clients/connection).

```ts
wsSupervisorGenerated({
  module: Example.module,
  config: {
    DbConnection,
    uri,
    databaseName,
    token: fetchFreshToken, // a string, or an Effect run for every attempt
    connectTimeoutMillis: 10_000,
    automaticReconnect: { delayMillisMin: 1_000, delayMillisMax: 30_000 },
  },
  setup: registerPresence,
  onAutomaticReconnect: registerPresence,
})
```

- The session outlives the drop: until the SDK has reconnected and re-applied
  every subscription the session holds, reads return the last rows and streams
  stay open, calls fail unsent with `CallNotSentError`, and calls in flight at
  the drop fail with `ConnectionLostError` (outcome unknown).
- The session ends when the SDK schedules no further attempt, when a reconnect
  comes back under a different identity (`ConnectionIdentityChangedError`),
  when a token refresh fails, or when an attempt or its replay is still
  unresolved `connectTimeoutMillis` after its scheduled start.
- `token` may be an Effect (`WsToken`), evaluated for each acquisition, every
  session a supervisor builds, and each SDK token refresh, so a long-lived
  client never reconnects with a token captured once. It must return a token
  that is not due for refresh, and never the one it returned last.
- Under a supervisor the phase is `recovering` (with the SDK's
  `reconnectAttempt`, `reconnectDelayMillis` and `reason`) while the SDK
  reconnects, and the same session is published as waiting.
  `onAutomaticReconnect` runs after every automatic reconnect, before the
  session is `live` again, to redo per-connection server state such as
  presence. An identity change parks the supervisor in `fatal`.
- The default retry policy is exported as `wsSupervisorIsRetryableDefault`, so
  a policy that parks on failures of its own can keep the default's:
  `isRetryable: (failure) => !mine(failure) && wsSupervisorIsRetryableDefault(failure)`.

## New: views with arguments

SpacetimeDB 2.13 lets a view take parameters. Declare them as a struct, as for
a reducer; the handler receives the decoded arguments:

```ts
Stdb.StdbFn.anonymousView("postsByAuthor", {
  params: Stdb.struct({ authorId: Stdb.string() }),
  returns: Stdb.array(post.row, { minimum: 0, maximum: 1_000 }),
})

postsByAuthor: Effect.fn(function* ({ authorId }) {
  const db = yield* ReadonlyDb
  return yield* db.post.byAuthor.filterToArray(authorId)
})
```

A client subscribes to a call. `targets.views.postsByAuthor` is now a function
of the arguments, and `viewGroup`, `streamViewRows` and `waitUntilView` take
them under `args`, which the types require exactly when a view has params:

```ts
session.viewGroup(["postsByAuthor", "allPosts"] as const, {
  args: { postsByAuthor: { authorId } },
})
```

The client sends `SELECT * FROM "posts_by_author"('…')`, encoding each argument
through the WebSocket codec and writing it as a SQL literal in the order the
params struct declares its fields. The host computes one answer per distinct
argument tuple (per caller, for a sender view). What SpacetimeDB 2.13 allows,
and so what this release enforces:

- A param must be a `bool`, an integer, a `string`, an `identity`, a
  `connectionId` or a `uuid`; anything else fails validation with
  `UnsupportedViewParam`. SpacetimeDB also accepts timestamps and byte arrays,
  which this release does not render yet.
- The rows of a view with params carry no primary key, so a changed row
  arrives as a delete and an insert.
- Every call a connection holds answers into the view's one client cache,
  which holds the union of their rows without saying which call produced each.
  Return the columns that carry the arguments if you subscribe to more than
  one call of a view.
- Arguments are positional, so reordering a view's params is a breaking
  change to the view.

`Stdb.structFields(type)` returns a struct value type's fields (or `undefined`
for any other type), and a `ViewSubscriptionTarget` now carries the call's
`params` and `args`.

## New: inter-database calls

SpacetimeDB 2.14 lets one database call another's reducers: the caller inserts
a row into an outbox table, the host delivers it once the transaction commits,
and a settle reducer on the caller sees the outcome. The contract now declares
all three, and codegen produces the binding the caller compiles against. See
[Inter-Database Calls](https://effect-stdb.dev/core-concepts/functions/inter-database-calls).

```ts
// Shared by both sides: the receivers one database exposes.
const Inbox = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Inbox", { errors: Stdb.errors(Refused) }).add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.receiver("receiveNote", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ note: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)
const InboxInterface = Stdb.RemoteInterface.make({ name: "inbox", group: Inbox })

// The caller: one outbox per receiver, one settle reducer per outbox.
const noteOutbox = Stdb.outboxTable("noteOutbox", {
  interface: InboxInterface,
  reducer: "receiveNote",
})
Stdb.StdbFn.outboxResult("noteSettled", { table: noteOutbox })

// The caller's module entry: the generated, committed binding loads only in a
// SpacetimeDB host, so only the entry imports it.
build(CallerModule, impls, {
  runtimeMode: "dev-guarded",
  receiverBindings: [Stdb.RemoteInterface.bind(InboxInterface, inboxBinding)],
})
```

- `Stdb.StdbFn.receiver` declares a reducer another database calls. Its wire
  name is pinned to `snakeCase(key)` and every name reachable from its params
  must be one lowercase word, so the call's signature does not depend on
  either module's case policy. A group that implements a receiver must declare
  a guard as `middleware.reducers`, and `StdbServer.databaseCaller(ctx)` gives
  that guard the calling database's host-signed identity.
- `Stdb.outboxTable` lays out the call row (`msgId`, `target`, the receiver's
  parameters, your own local columns, `enqueuedAt`) with a `byTarget` index.
  The insert handle refuses a row over its `rowBytesMax` (64 KiB by default,
  1 MiB at most) with the typed `OutboxRowTooLarge`, and dies on a row
  addressed to the database itself or sent outside a reducer or procedure
  transaction. A target is a `PeerIdentity` that only
  `Stdb.RemoteInterface.peer` mints.
- `Stdb.StdbFn.outboxResult` declares the settle reducer. Its handler gets the
  row and an `OutboxResult` (`Delivered`, or `Refused` with the receiver's
  failure text), cannot fail at the type level, and refuses any caller but the
  host. Its group's `middleware.reducers` does not run for it: the middleware
  is for the group's other callers, and would refuse the host.
- `generateReceiverArtifact` and `checkReceiverArtifact` in
  `effect-spacetimedb/codegen` run native `spacetime generate --bindings
  module` and commit the binding quarantined like a generated client.
- `Stdb.RemoteInterface.make({ name, group })` names the interface in the
  contract, which stays importable outside a SpacetimeDB host.
  `Stdb.RemoteInterface.bind(interface, binding)` pairs it with its binding in
  the calling module's entry and checks the binding against the receivers;
  `build`'s `receiverBindings` takes the pairs and refuses an outbox whose
  interface has none.
- `StdbServer.outboxBacklog(rows, now)` groups an outbox's pending rows by
  target, with each target's count and oldest row's age, so a module can tell
  a stuck stream from a slow one.
- `StdbTesting.makeIdcPump` delivers outbox rows between module harnesses in
  memory, one stream at a time, so a test chooses every interleaving. A
  harness takes a `databaseIdentity` (linked harnesses need distinct ones) and
  lists an outbox's pending rows with `outboxRows(key)`.
- The dev server publishes several databases on one standalone
  (`runtime.publishDatabase`), reports each one's `databaseIdentity`, removes
  one (`remove`), and adds `localhost` to every standalone's `NO_PROXY`: the
  host posts deliveries to `http://localhost:<port>` and honors the proxy
  variables. `publishEnvironmentOnly` is exported.

Deliveries only reach a database on the same host as the caller, and the host
retries a failed transport without end: a missing target, a connection hook
that refuses the caller, or a row too large for the host holds that stream's
later rows forever. The owner can read each pending row's `retry_count` and
`last_transport_error` from `st_outbound_msg` over SQL.

## Also in this release

- `Stdb.identityEquals` and `normalizeIdentity` accept the `Identity` instances
  a host passes a module (`ctx.sender`, `ctx.identity`). A module bundle holds
  a second copy of the SDK's `Identity` class, from its server entry, and
  before this release comparing one of those with anything returned `false`.
  A plain record with an `__identity__` field is still refused.
  `Stdb.ScheduleAt.at` likewise accepts the host's `ctx.timestamp`, which 0.7
  could not convert for the same reason.
- A lifecycle hook's `StdbSenderFailure` now reaches the host as SpacetimeDB's
  `SenderError`, as a reducer's already did: a `clientConnected` or `init` that
  refuses its caller is answered as a refusal with your message, where 0.7 made
  the host report that the instance encountered a fatal error.
- WebSocket sessions notice a dead connection sooner. Releasing a session
  invalidates its connection before disconnecting, so calls still in flight,
  or made later through a stale handle, fail with `ConnectionLostError`
  instead of waiting forever. Every call, subscribe and `isInvalidated()`
  first checks the SDK's `isSocketClosed`, so a socket the browser tore down
  without a close event (a frozen tab, a sleeping machine) invalidates the
  connection on the next read. A supervised live session is re-checked when
  the page becomes visible, regains focus, comes back online or is restored
  from the back-forward cache, and `unsubscribeThen` settles once the
  connection carrying the subscription is lost.
- The module test harness gains `reset()`, which empties every table and
  restarts the sequences, the uuid counter and the random stream (a rollback
  restores rows only), for suites that want a fresh database per call. Its raw
  `db` is now typed `TestModuleRawDb`, which matches what it holds: host column
  values, so a column with a domain schema reads there as its encoded type. Use
  `effectDb` for decoded rows.
- Every integer constructor (`Stdb.u8(domain)` to `Stdb.i256(domain)`)
  accepts a domain schema whose decoded type is not itself a number or bigint,
  such as a value object that encodes to one, and row refs and row atoms key
  a value that implements Effect `Equal` with a string `key()` by that key. The
  root exports `HostValue`, `HostOf`, `HostStruct`, `HostSum` and the
  `HostValueTypeId` symbol, which describe the SDK's host-side shape of a
  value type.
- The dev server takes `standaloneEnvironment`, variables set on the
  standalone server process, for example to route procedure HTTP through a
  proxy.
- Building the message of a `StdbDecodeError` or a call error no longer throws
  when its cause is a null-prototype record or cannot be serialized; the
  cause is rendered structurally instead.
- `ArtifactDriftError` gains `artifact` (`"generated client"` or
  `"receiver binding"`), and client generation runs the CLI with
  `--no-config`, so a `spacetime.json` above the working directory no longer
  adds targets to the run.
- The optional `esbuild` peer that codegen needs accepts 0.25 through 0.28
  (it was `^0.25`), so a project on a current esbuild installs without a peer
  conflict. A generated artifact's banner records the esbuild version, so
  regenerating with another one shows as drift.
- The HTTP JSON client rejects response bodies nested deeper than 128
  array/object levels with its existing typed decode error (`StdbDecodeError`).
  Deeper bodies previously recursed without a bound and overflowed the stack
  on V8 at roughly 450 levels. 128 equals the host's `serde_json` limit on
  HTTP arguments, so anything you can send you can also receive; the only
  values it newly refuses are recursive (`Stdb.lazy`) return values nested more
  than 128 levels deep, for example a tree with more than 64 nodes on one path.
